SELECTOR AMBIGUITY (fixable, does not flip outcome): the element-under-test selector `table.parallel[role="presentation"]` matches TWO tables in the document (the header-only table at HTML lines 29-34 and the poem table at lines 52-69). querySelector resolves to the FIRST one — confirmed by inspect.js, which reported the matched element's text as 'Español\nEnglish' and innerHTML containing only the colhead row. The element that actually carries the F49 interleave is the SECOND table, so the recorded selector points at the wrong element. Fix: disambiguate (e.g. `table.parallel:nth-of-type(2)` / `:last-of-type`, or merge into one table).

MINOR title/H1 mismatch (cosmetic, not the tested issue): <title> and scenario quote the first line 'Caminante, son tus huellas' but the <h1> reads 'Caminante, no hay camino' (a different line of the same poem). Does not affect the 1.3.2 verdict.

Minor prose/citation framing slip: the .md and HTML comments foreground F49's NESTED-table trap ('the screen reader reads the entire nested table before moving on'), but the photo's nested table is a trivial single-cell wrapper that contributes nothing to the separation. The actual sequence break is driven by inner-table ROW order (row 1 = photo+full-text-block, row 2 = caption), i.e. the G57 'caption in the row following the illustration' mechanism. The primary citation (G57) describes the real mechanism exactly, so the verdict is unaffected, but the F49 nested-table emphasis is somewhat of a red herring.

This is a deliberate CONTROL / PASS trap, not a failure case: there is intentionally no accessibility error. errorIsReal=false reflects that there is no issue to confirm; the page's documented mechanism is explicitly 'none — control case'. expectedOutcomeCorrect=true because the page genuinely yields the documented 'passed' outcome.

Minor (not a defect, just a fidelity caveat): F32's literal failure example uses regular spaces ('W e l c o m e'); this page uses   (U+00A0), which the technique covers in a sibling note ('  can also be used to add white space, producing similar failures') — so it is in scope, but it is the   variant rather than the headline example.

Minor: real-world screen-reader behavior with U+00A0 between letters is engine-dependent (some normalize/announce 'Welcome', some spell out). The F32 deterministic test procedure still marks it a failure, so the 'failed' label is correct, but the claimed 'reads letter-by-letter' is engine-dependent rather than universal.

Minor (non-blocking) wording nit: the in-page summary at html line 71 calls the word "都道府県名 「東京都」" where 都道府県名 means 'prefecture name', which is slightly awkward framing of the lexeme inside the <code> callout; it is descriptive prose, not a citation, and does not affect the 1.3.2 outcome.

They pass not because they ARE initialisms per se, but because their MARKUP contains no intra-word whitespace ( /spaces inside a word), so F32 simply does not apply. The carve-out still holds and the contrast is valid.

The doc honestly labels it an 'F33 variant', and F33's own title ('using white space characters to create multiple columns in plain text content') covers the whitespace-fakes-a-positional-grid principle, so the citation supports the mechanism. No correction required.

No defect. This is a correctly-constructed boundary PASS / negative control for 1.3.2; the documented outcome 'passed' is accurate and no 1.3.2 error is present (errorIsReal=false is the intended state for a pass control).

None material. Minor SC-framing nuance (not a defect, worth noting): the strict normative text of SC 1.3.2 only requires that 'a correct reading sequence can be programmatically determined' — which IS satisfied here (DOM/AX order is 7.1,7.2,7.3 and a pure screen-reader user gets the correct sequence). The 'failed' verdict rests on the Trusted Tester Test 15.A DOM-vs-visual interpretation and WCAG C27/F1 technique framing (visual reading order of meaning-bearing content must match DOM order), which the doc cites correctly. A purist could argue the harm to sighted-mobile/magnifier users sits at the 1.3.2/1.4.10 boundary, but the corpus's cited authority (Trusted Tester) clearly scopes it to 1.3.2. No correction needed.

Minor (non-blocking) measurement nuance: a naive top-then-left reading-order heuristic returns the SAME visual order `m1,tip,m2` at BOTH desktop and mobile widths (verified: desktop tip.top=224 same row as m1, sorts before m2; mobile tip.top=364 between). The true desktop-vs-mobile distinction is column structure (desktop: tip is a parallel right column, tip.left=684 >= m1.right=661, tipBesideM1=true; mobile: single 458px column, tipBesideM1=false, tip vertically interleaved). The doc's 'tip beside m1/m2 on desktop, interleaved on mobile' framing is correct, but a crude geometric checker could misread desktop as also broken — the real signal is multi-column flow + prose continuity, which only reinforces that this needs human judgment. Not a defect in the case, just a caution against trusting a naive linearizer.

The doc cites TWO references (Understanding 1.3.2 Example 1 column-flow + F1 Description). The prompt's 'Claimed citation' field names only F1. Both are verbatim and supportive; no conflict, noted for completeness.

Pure-SC-1.3.2 nuance (not a defect, but worth noting): the SC's core test is whether a *meaningful programmatic* sequence can be determined. Here the DOM/AX/tab order is Previous>Play>Next (correct, matches the caption), so the programmatic sequence itself PASSES. The genuine failure is the Technique C27 visual-vs-source divergence: at <=560px the rendered visual order (Next>Play>Previous) contradicts the prose caption and arrow glyphs. This is a recognized 1.3.2 *failure pattern* and the cited technique (C27) is exactly the right one, but the primary harmed user is the sighted/low-vision/magnifier user, not the blind screen-reader user (who, per the doc itself line 46-47, gets a consistent correct order). The label 'failed' is defensible under the C27 framing; reviewers should know the screen-reader-only experience is fine.

Both citations verified VERBATIM and correctly attributed: C27 'A keyboard user may have trouble predicting where focus will go next when the source order does not match the visual order.' appears verbatim at wcag-techniques/css/C27.html line 20; Understanding-1.3.2 'It is important that it be possible to programmatically determine at least one sequence of the content that makes sense.' appears verbatim at wcag-understanding/meaningful-sequence.html lines 25-28. No hallucination.

The trap is still valid but is about prominence, not raw spatial reading order — worth keeping the wording precise.

In reality float:right is INERT on a flex item, and order:99 + the sibling

rule flex:1 1 100% wraps the aside onto its own flex line at the END of the container. Measured boxes: part-a top404/bottom465, part-b top483/bottom544 (contiguous, full width), aside top784/bottom986/left48-338 (bottom-LEFT, below the whole body). Minor (non-blocking): the F1 reference's literal example uses position:absolute, while this case uses flexbox `order:`. F1's description text and SC 1.3.2 both cover any CSS-vs-programmatic-order mismatch, so the citation still supports the mechanism; flex `order` is a valid modern instance of the same failure. Not a defect, just a note.
